title: Constitutional Amendment Requiring Limits on Property Tax Increases by Local Governments

context.text: Referred to the ballot by the General Assembly as House Bill 1089 (Session Law 2026-5), ratified May 21, 2026; primary sponsors include Rep. Brian Echevarria (R-Cabarrus). The third-reading roll calls were 73-46 in the House and 31-15 in the Senate. North Carolina governors have no veto over proposed amendments.

question.text: [ ] FOR [ ] AGAINST Constitutional amendment requiring limits on property tax increases by local governments.

summary.text: The amendment would amend Article V, Section 2(5) of the North Carolina Constitution to add: "The General Assembly shall enact general laws limiting the amount by which the levy of taxes on property may increase, which may include exceptions." It does not itself set a limit; it requires the General Assembly to pass general laws setting one, and allows exceptions. If approved, it takes effect upon certification of the vote by the State Board of Elections. The session law contains no fiscal estimate; the NC Budget & Tax Center and legislators cited differing estimates of household savings (see arguments).

measure.yesMeans: Adds to the state Constitution a requirement that the General Assembly enact general laws limiting how much local governments' property tax levies may increase, which may include exceptions.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the Constitution unchanged; the General Assembly would not be constitutionally required to enact limits on increases in local property tax levies.

argumentsFor.text: House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Caldwell) said: "Property taxes are out of control, and some local governments are abusing their power by overtaxing and underdelivering for their constituents. It's time for real reform, and this constitutional amendment on levy limits will help stop runaway property tax hikes and protect North Carolina taxpayers."

Rep. Brian Echevarria (R-Cabarrus), a primary sponsor, said: "The resulting debate led to the conclusion that asking the people whether they want a constitutional amendment requiring limits on property tax increases by local governments is the next step toward a modern, fairer, and more predictable property tax system."

argumentsAgainst.text: Alexandra Sirota, executive director of the NC Budget & Tax Center, said: "A levy limit will not address the unaffordable housing costs that so many households are facing. What legislators need to do today is to invest in building more affordable housing and providing direct relief to households that are faced with unaffordable property tax bills."

Rep. Deb Butler (D-New Hanover) said: "The truth is, property taxes are not rising because cities and counties suddenly went on a wild, drunken binge and started spending like sailors. It's because of the cost shifting that we have done from this body." She said reforms to existing property tax relief programs could yield savings of up to $6,000 for some households, compared with about $300 from a levy limit.

currentLaw.text: Article V, Section 2(5) of the North Carolina Constitution currently bars the General Assembly from authorizing local governments to levy property taxes except for purposes authorized by general law uniformly applicable throughout the State, unless approved by a majority of the unit's voters; it contains no requirement to limit levy increases. There is no state property tax in North Carolina; counties and municipalities set the rates.

fiscalImpact.text: The Fiscal Research Division (May 5, 2026 fiscal note on H.B. 1089) estimated no fiscal impact: the bill only holds a referendum, the specifics of any levy limit would be set in later legislation and addressed by a future fiscal note, and election costs are anticipated to be minimal.

supporters.text: House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Caldwell) said property taxes are out of control and some local governments are overtaxing.
Rep. Brian Echevarria (R-Cabarrus), a primary sponsor, said North Carolinians deserve a chance to reform the property tax system.

opponents.text: Alexandra Sirota, executive director of the NC Budget & Tax Center, said a levy limit will not address unaffordable housing costs.
NC By the People, a ballot referendum committee of 20 organizations, is campaigning against all three amendments, including this one.
North Carolina Association of Educators, a coalition member, was quoted in the coalition's release saying the amendments would gut county budgets that fund schools.

researchNotes: Ballot question text is taken verbatim from the question set out in the ratified session law, which is the text the State Board of Elections is directed to use on ballots. The North Carolina State Board of Elections' certified list could not be loaded (its pages list no ballot-question text); the three statewide amendments rest on the session laws and WUNC's September 22, 2026 explainer, which says voters will decide three proposed amendments, and the question wording is taken from the session laws. North Carolina has no citizen initiative and publishes no voter-pamphlet arguments; arguments are attributed quotes from news reports. A simple majority of votes cast on the question approves each amendment. No registered ballot-measure committees were identified in the sources reviewed. Supporters and opponents are limited to those whose stance a fetched page shows. No campaign-finance totals for the ballot-measure committees were found, so campaignFinance is omitted.
